Strategic tree planting should  be a priority for the myriad benefits provided (e.g., shade,  carbon sequestration, stormwater management, etc.). In the immediate and short term, however, shade structures and pavilions should also be provided, as trees will take years  before reaching maturity and offering the benefits of shade.  Larger pavilions intended for rentals for groups/special events can both encourage use of parks and help offset costs of providing shade structures. CPTED (Crime Prevention Through Environ- mental Design) An important component of keeping spaces safe and free of vandalism is fostering a strong sense of belonging as well as the belief that parks and recreation facilities are owned and cared for by all members of the community. Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) is a multi-disciplinary crime prevention approach that uses architecture, urban planning, and facility management to reduce crime opportunities and fear of crime through strategies intended to build a sense of community.   1   The principles of First Generation CPTED include:  Territoriality/territorial control:   Locate public spaces near residential areas where residents already come to associate the spaces around their homes as their own.  Natural surveillance:   Encourage the ability for onlookers to casually observe activity in public spaces through clear sightlines, lighting, landscaping (i.e., clearing bushes, shrubs, and overgrowth). Holding activities and programming in public spaces also increases natural surveillance.  1   https://www.cpted.net/Primer-in-CPTED  Image and milieu:   Support residents in getting to know their neighbours, and maintain a positive image of an area (e.g.,  beautification, litter clean-ups).  Access control:   Introduce road barriers or landscaping to control frontage in the creation of mini-neighbourhoods. The principles of Second Generation CPTED include:  Social cohesion:   Enhance positive social relations/groups between residents of a neighbourhood focused on solving local problems (e.g., promote activities, interaction, collaboration).  Community culture:   Convene people to create a common sense of purpose and form a strong bond (e.g., cultural events, art and music festival, placemaking and placekeeping activities).  Connectivity:   Promote inclusivity among all neighbourhoods and groups regardless of ethnicity, income, gender, age, ability (e.g., communication, linked walkways, events shared by multiple neighbourhoods)  Threshold capacity:   Embrace genuine diversity in the range of community uses (e.g., parks, amenities, food outlets, recreation buildings). Employing CPTED in parks, facilities, and trails will both foster safety, and discourage vandalism. The recovery objectives are based on the financial  capacity of the municipality to provide all the services within its mandate, given available budgets and the need for judicious spending. Pricing for parks and recreation services would be part of a corporate-wide policy. The following discussion is limited to parks and recreation services. As noted in Table 5-1, the City intends to develop a pricing strategy. While municipal recreation services are typically subsidized to some degree, the extent of cost recovery in various areas of service should be rationalized in terms of cost-  benefit. There are currently no parameters in place to identify  the point at which programs and services should be charged at higher fees or are not viable to operate. For programs, for example, it is important to be able to determine minimum levels of enrollment/registration needed to offer a program, based on the costs to deliver it in relation to pre-determined recovery rates. Although not-for-profit community groups or organizations  must be registered to receive municipal assistance, registration does not guarantee support. A standard, typically annual, registration/ application process for eligible  groups interested in municipal assistance “affiliates” them  with the municipality and establishes a formal, consistent process for reviewing requests and monitoring policy effectiveness. Municipal staff review the applications and make recommendations to Council for approval. The support provided is typically in- kind, with any major funding provided through a separate mechanism.  The policy specifies criteria for affiliation and the services available to affiliated groups. The legislation revised ten provincial Acts including but not limited to the Conservation Authorities Act, Development Charges Act,  and Planning Act, which resulted in significant implications  for Ontario’s land use planning regime. Bill 23 overrides zoning by-laws to increase density but simultaneously limits municipalities’ ability to use development charges and parkland requirements toward concurrent infrastructure and services that support that density. For municipalities experiencing residential growth, adherence to Bill 23 has a disproportionate  impact on finances. Specifically, parkland dedication caps have been altered under  Bill 23 such that the maximum alternative rate was cut in half from 1 hectare per 300 dwelling units to 1 hectare per 600 net residential units; likewise, the cash-in-lieu parkland rate for medium- and high-density developments was cut in half from 1 hectare per 500 dwelling units to 1 hectare per 1,000  net residential units. Sites of five hectares or larger are now capped at 15% parkland dedication, while sites less than five  hectares are capped at 10% parkland dedication. Municipalities  Page 375 of 983 April 2024 181 7.0 I m p l e m e n t a t i o n  must also accept encumbered lands (e.g., land with below- grade infrastructure) or privately-owned publicly-accessible open spaces (POPS) as parkland conveyance. Similarly, Bill 23 reduces the amount of development charges permitted under municipalities’ existing and future development charges by-laws. Development charges for rental housing units have been further reduced. Municipalities can no longer use development charges to purchase land for growth-related infrastructure or fund planning studies or assessments. In addition, a variety of new housing units  – affordable, attainable, non-profit, and inclusionary zoning  housing units, as well as gentle density (up to three units per lot) and rental buildings with four or more units – are exempt from development charges and parkland dedication fees.  Revised definitions of these housing typologies may result in  larger proportions of housing supply considered eligible for these exemptions. Consequently, the revenue shortfalls resulting from Bill  23 present significant challenges to delivering current,  planned, and future infrastructure necessary in residential communities. The quality and location of new parkland and facilities will be compromised, with fewer amenities, pressure to collaborate on shared space, and more reliance placed on the existing parks system. Other revenue-generating tools,  innovative financing, and collaborative partnerships will be crucial for Sault to address financial deficiencies and create complete communities with sufficient park and recreation  amenities and facilities. In this regard, all participants have the right to utilize the dressing room or appropriate and equivalent dressing environment based on their gender identity, religious beliefs, body image concerns and/or other reasons related to their individual needs. Hockey Canada believes in balancing the safety, privacy, modesty and wishes of our participants without compromising the aspects of camaraderie, social integration and bonding inherent in a team sport. This Policy attempts to meet these goals while providing a safe and respectful environment for participants. This Policy represents a shift in philosophy from previous dressing room regulations. As will be further explained below, this new model is based upon creating safe, inclusive and equitable dressing room environments that are designated team spaces for everyone, while providing proper supervision.  SCOPE The Dressing Room Policy applies to all minor hockey teams sanctioned by Hockey Canada and its Members. DEFINITIONS  •   “ Dressing rooms ” –   officially designated spaces for changing in and out of gear. Mostly, these are  men’s and women’s, multi -stall spaces and occasionally can be all-gender, multi-stall spaces.  •   “ Dressing environments ” –   spaces beyond dressing rooms (in close proximity to them) that can be temporarily repurposed to provide a space for a small number of participants to change in and out  of their gear (e.g., official’s room, multi -purpose room, meeting rooms, single-unit washrooms).  •   “ Policy ” –   means this Dressing Room Policy.  PROCEDURE  The Minimum Attire Rule  To best promote inclusion and to respect the privacy of all participants on a team, Hockey Canada requires  all participants to wear ‘minimum attire’ at all times in a dressing room or in dressing environments where  more than one participant is present. This means that participants should arrive at the rink wearing a base layer (e.g., shorts and t-shirt, compression shorts and shirt or sports bra). A participant not arriving at the rink wearing their base layer can use an appropriate private space (e.g., private restroom stalls or empty/unused dressing rooms) to change into the base layer and then enter the team dressing room with the other participants. Page 398 of 983 City of Sault Ste. Marie | Parks and Recreation Master Plan 204 DRESSING ROOM POLICY  It is the responsibility of all coaches and team staff to instruct players regarding the minimum attire rule and ensure that players are complying with this Policy. Hockey Canada recognizes the physical limitations of some facilities and encourages associations to work creatively and proactively, using an athlete-focused, ethical, and values-based approach, with local facility management to ensure that appropriate and equivalent dressing environments are available to all participants who would prefer not to get dressed in the team dressing room.  Team Talks  Hockey Canada stresses the importance that all participants are treated as valued members of a team. Therefore, coaches and team staff should only engage in pre- and post-game talks when all athletes are present in the dressing room.  Use of Showers   –   Recommended Best Practice  As outlined in the purpose section, there are many reasons why athletes may require privacy (religious reasons, chronic conditions, body image, gender). The following guidance around the use of showers, is an additional step in creating environments within which athletes feel safe and secure. It is recommended that when showers are not private stalls, that these be used in a manner that respects the privacy of all participants.   When in open concept showers, it is encouraged that all athletes wear certain “minimum  attire ” at all times, including swimwear.   In order to facilitate this, participants could use a private restroom stall to change out of their base layer and into their swimwear prior to using the shower. Similarly, they could dress in a private restroom stall after they have completed their shower. Coaches and/or team staff should ensure they are able to supervise the dressing room while participants are  showering, following ‘Rule of Two’ guidelines below.  Officials Dressing Rooms  Given that dressing room spaces for officials and officiating teams are often shared by officials of a wide variety of ages and genders and may be used by different sports at the same time, safety and privacy are of the utmost importance. To create a safe and welcoming environment for everyone who uses an officials dressing room space, the minimum attire rule and shower recommendations described should be applied.  Applicable Laws  Hockey Canada Members that have mediated human rights settlements within their Province/Territory with respect to specific dressing room parameters are exempted from this Policy within their jurisdictions, but solely to the extent required so that they may continue to adhere to such settlements. The ‘Rule of Two’ requires  two trained and screened adults to be present in the dressing room or immediately outside the dressing room with the door propped open to monitor the environment and ensure it is free of any discrimination, harassment, bullying, or other forms of maltreatment. The Rule of Two remains in place when showers are in use.  Prohibition on Violent Activities in Dressing Rooms  To ensure the safety of all participants in the dressing room, no type of violent conduct of any kind  (including locker room boxing) bullying, or hazing is permitted. It is the responsibility of coaches and team staff to ensure that no such violent behaviour is taking place in dressing rooms or dressing environments. Should anyone experience maltreatment in violation of this section of the Policy, a complaint may be submitted to   Hockey Canada’s Independent Third Party .  Prohibition on Recording in Dressing Rooms or Dressing Environments  To respect the privacy of participants, no videos, still photos, or voice recordings of any kind may be taken using any device with recording capabilities in a dressing room or dressing environment. Cell phones are only permitted to be used in a dressing room or dressing environment for the purposes of controlling music played in those spaces. The Dressing Room Policy is focused on enhancing inclusion and safety for all participants on any team or officiating team across the country. What this means is that all interactions with athletes need to be conducted in open, observable and justifiable environments, which applies to dressing rooms. More information on the Rule of Two is available in the Hockey Canada Screening Policy.  3.   What are open, observable and justifiable environments?  a.   Sport environments that are open, observable and justifiable refer to those that occur that are normal to a sport environment (i.e. arena, workout facilities, dressing rooms, bench, ice surface) that allow individuals to view the environment and do not typically occur behind closed doors. The idea is that all interactions with athletes occur in a location that someone could interrupt if necessary.  4.   How does the Rule of Two work within a dressing room environment?  a.   Fundamentally, the Rule of Two is designed for all communication and interaction to be conducted in an open, observable and justifiable environment. The dressing room by its design is not always open or observable, but the environment is justifiable in the sport context. To abide by the principles of the Rule of Two, interaction with participants can occur within the dressing room if two screened and trained team officials, volunteers or parents/guardians are present with the dressing room.  5.   What is a trained and screened individual?  a.   Trained and screened is defined by the Coaching Association of Canada (CAC) as individuals who have completed ethics education (Respect in Sport or CAC Safe Sport Training) and have passed a thorough background check, which can include items like interviews, criminal record checks and reference checks.  6.   Why should the Rule of Two be implemented?  a.   The Rule of Two is designed to provide greater protection to both athletes and team staff/ coaches by never leaving two individuals where there is a power imbalance present alone. Intensification is the development of a property, site, or area at a higher density than currently exists, through redevelopment, the development of vacant or underutilized lots, infill, and the expansion or conversion of existing buildings. Intensification is essential to completing our neighbourhoods, making the most efficient use of land, resources, infrastructure and public service facilities, minimizing negative impacts on air quality and climate change, promoting energy efficiency and supporting public transit, active transportation and the efficient movement of people and goods.  The   City’s   SDAs   comprise   the   first   settlement   area   of   the   City   (including  Downtown) and areas within a safe-walkable distance to an array of services and amenities such as retail clusters, grocery stores, community centres, schools, and  parks. This area contains a large employment concentration and is   the   location   of   the   highest   density   of   office   developments.   The   First Neighbourhoods should be the primary focus of intensification and revitalization activities, thereby helping the area continue to become a vibrant, resilient and diverse mixed-use residential community that provides a range of housing options for   all   residents. COMMENTS Population Growth and Housing Supply  Sault Ste. Marie’s Housing Needs Assessment 2023 -2025 projects that the City will add around 8,400 new residents over the next 12 to 15 years; primarily through migration. This identifies a need to increase the overall supply of housing units within the City to meet near and long-term housing demand. The Province has established a target of 1,500 new housing units by 2031, while the Assessment demonstrates a need of 3,115 new housing units by 2036. To meet both targets, the City must ensure there is an overall increase in the supply of housing. In recent years, the housing stock of the City has not kept up with demand. Not enough rental units were built between 2016 and 2021, contributing to supply challenges and lowering the rental vacancy rate to near historic levels. New rental unit supply is needed and should be a mix of purposely-built affordable units and moderately   priced   units   within   walkable   and   well   connected   urban neighbourhoods. If the supply of moderately priced units is increased, some portion of rental units in older buildings will filter down-market and become affordable for households with lower incomes. More freehold housing is also required as market ownership housing has not kept up with demand, largely due to the rising costs of construction. It is critical that the city has enough housing supply to accommodate this growth, both affordable and market rate.  Intensification  Intensification is a key strategy to accommodate and support the long-term demand for residential housing in the City. The City of Sault Ste. Marie has identified Strategic Development Areas (SDAs), or areas that are proposed to be  Page 420 of 983 A-5-24-OP Strategic Development Areas May 13, 2024 Page 10. the focus for intensification and higher-density mixed uses. The SDAs are shown on the map in Appendix A. The benefits of intensification include:     Maximizing the use of municipal infrastructure and services   –   more compact forms of development make better use of land and existing infrastructure, which includes roads and municipal services such as transit, underground utilities, community centres, and facilities.     Increasing community efficiency, support existing and new services and businesses   –   residential intensification and mixed-use development in areas with amenities, services, and healthy food retailers contributes to creating complete neighbourhoods where residents live within walking distance of a variety of needs. Intensification, when focused to specific areas, will add population to support local businesses and may also create new jobs within them.     Reducing urban sprawl   –   infill development in existing neighbourhoods means less greenfield space is required for new housing development and avoids the need for costly extensions of infrastructure and services.     Supporting   the   use   of   public   transit   and   active   modes   of transportation   –   infill development contributes to greater densities, which are transit supportive and promote walking and cycling.     Encouraging environmental sustainability   –   can reduce dependence on automobiles, minimizing impacts on air quality, and promoting energy efficiency.     Create   more   housing   choices   and   improve   affordability   –   mixed residential neighbourhoods are those with a variety of housing types and tenures available to a variety of people at different life stages. Infill units, converted dwellings, and second units are often those which are most affordably priced. Intensification will be encouraged in the SDAs in a number of ways. These include:     The   provision   of   financial   incentives   for   housing   development through a Housing Community Improvement Plan (CIP)   –   financial incentives   may   include   municipal   fee   rebates,   per-door   grants,   tax increment equivalent grants (TIEGs), and housing feasibility studies for Not- for-Profit landowners. The City proposes to offer higher grant or rebate values for developments on lands within the SDAs than those on lands outside of the SDAs. Furthermore, developments located in an SDA may be able to take advantage of several grants/programs (stacking), while those outside of SDAs may not. All financial incentives for housing will consider whether the development will contain some (or all) units that meet the definition of "affordable housing", which is focused on the missing middle.  Page 421 of 983 A-5-24-OP Strategic Development Areas May 13, 2024 Page 11.     Reductions to parking requirements   –   will facilitate higher development densities,   unlock   additional   development   potential   within   existing developments, and potentially lower development costs. Higher-density mixed-use   neighbourhoods   within   a   safe-walkable   access   to   public transportation, services, and amenities may have relatively lower per-unit parking requirements compared to areas with primarily lower densities. Also, commercial or institutional lands with large parking lots may free up lands that could be used for additional development (including housing), the majority of which are located in SDAs.     Advance housing on government land   –   through the Housing CIP, the City will grant or sell municipally owned land that has been declared surplus to applicants intending on constructing housing. Although this program will be available throughout the Urban Settlement Area, priority will be placed on identifying and divesting properties within the SDAs. The City will also engage with public entities to identify surplus public lands and ensure that the disposal of any surplus and/or underutilized public land prioritizes the provision of affordable housing.     Improve the active transportation network   –   ensure that streets facilitate pedestrian and cyclist modes of travel and that the active transportation network consists of a mix of multi-use pathways, on-road cycling lanes, sidewalks and walkways. For example, the intersection of Goulais Avenue and Second Line West has higher density residential development nearby but few retail opportunities and no grocers within an 800m safe-walkable distance. Additional neighbourhood commercial near this intersection would contribute to filling a land use gap and would expand the existing West End SDA further west. Furthermore, pedestrian-friendly improvements in areas surrounding SDAs, such as the installation of Pedestrian Crossovers (PXOs) on arterial streets, may bring more properties into the SDA. For example, a pedestrian crossing of Wellington Street East near Nicolas Avenue / Hugill Street would improve pedestrian access to the Trunk Road commercial areas for properties south of Wellington and east of Lake Street. This may result in the East End SDA expanding to include the Algoma University area. The map in Appendix C shows areas (shaded in cyan) that have potential to become part of SDAs; however land use gaps currently exist. The map also lists the Other SDA inclusion criteria for each gap area, indicating what is nearby and what is missing. The initial exercise of identifying and establishing SDAs is meant to be a baseline of access to services and amenities from residential properties through safe, walkable routes. This analysis should be revisited in the future to see how scores have improved over time and to adjust the SDA boundaries if necessary.  CONSULTATION  Public notice was posted on the   City’s website on   April 19 and advertised in the Sault Star on April 20. An advertisement was posted on Sootoday, intermittently between April 29 and May 10. As this is a City-wide application, no physical notices were mailed out. Up to the drafting of this report, no comments were received as a result of the public notice process. As part of the Grow the Sault initiative, four public information sessions on SDAs occurred in November 2023. These sessions, promoted in online media, social media, and the City website, engaged approximately 80 members of the public. Also, a public consultation website dedicated to SDAs was posted to the web and linked through the Grow the Sault website. The site received 51 views and 6 participants left survey responses and comments.  Page 430 of 983 A-5-24-OP Strategic Development Areas May 13, 2024 Page 20. During these public information sessions and through the SDA website, many individuals expressed general agreement and support for the increased supply of diverse housing in areas near   services,   amenities,   the active   transportation network,   and   public   transportation.   Several   participants   indicated   that   infill development and intensification is a cost-effective way for the City to grow. A few participants indicated that the City should prioritize initiatives that increase the supply   of   housing;   specifically   commenting   that   rental   rates   have   become unaffordable. Staff also sought public feedback on the proposed SDA boundaries as well as the types of services and amenities that should be considered when establishing these boundaries. Several participants indicated that it was not appropriate to encourage intensification and increased population density in areas adjacent to Algoma Steel. Based   on   this   feedback,   the   geographic   coverage   of   the   proposed   First Neighbourhoods was reduced   in size.   Also,   the public consultation process affirmed that the services and amenities described above were suitable for inclusion. Grocery stores, health services, retail locations, and transit stops were considered to be the most important criteria for inclusion. A   few   participants   were   critical   of   the   proposed   SDAs;   commenting   that intensification and the permitting of denser forms of housing would negatively alter the character of their neighbourhood. This is a similar concern to those typically heard through rezoning applications involving denser development forms. It is important to note that smaller-scale residential intensification is already permitted in the Zoning By-law and any larger housing developments (with 11 or more dwelling units) will automatically trigger site plan control where applicable studies, such as traffic studies and servicing studies may be required. Furthermore, stakeholder feedback was sought through the Affordable Housing Task Force (AHTF). The SDA methodology and proposed boundaries were presented to the AHTF for comment and revision. Through this stakeholder consultation process, the geographic coverage of the First Neighbourhoods was reduced to the current proposed boundary. FINANCIAL IMPLICATIONS  The proposed amendments propose directing growth to existing areas of the city that are already serviced by infrastructure like roads, water, sewer, and other utilities. Directing growth from within rather than expanding outwards avoids the need for costly infrastructure expansion but may prompt the need to consider higher levels of service or upgrades to infrastructure that are located in areas that will experience a sizeable increase in population growth. The latter is typically still more cost effective than outward growth.  STRATEGIC PLAN / POLICY IMPACT  The proposed amendments support the following strategic focus areas of the corporate strategic plan. Maintaining   existing   infrastructure:   These   amendments   encourage   infill development and residential intensification within SDAs, thus promoting more efficient use of existing municipal infrastructure and services. Quality of Life: Increasing housing supply better ensures that residents have better access to affordable and diverse housing options. Affordable and adequate housing is a social determinant of health that influences one's quality of life. Vibrant Downtown Areas: These amendments encourage infill development within the First Neighbourhoods, which includes the Downtown. An increase in residential density in the Downtown can help create a vibrant, complete community where people want to live and work.  Climate Impact  Higher-density   mixed-use   development   within   the   City's   SDAs   fosters   an environment   conducive   to   active   transportation.   Compact,   mixed-use developments promote walkability, cycling, and public transit usage due to shorter distances between residences, workplaces, and amenities, thus reducing carbon emissions.  SUMMARY  A series of Official Plan amendments focusing on the establishment of Strategic Development Areas (SDAs) are being proposed. The SDAs are proposed to be  focus areas for accommodating a significant portion of the City’s growth   through intensification. Within the SDAs the City will encourage and support:     a complete mix of land uses with an emphasis on filling land use gaps and creating complete neighbourhoods that can meet a variety of needs, such as living, working, education, shopping, and recreational opportunities;  Page 432 of 983 A-5-24-OP Strategic Development Areas May 13, 2024 Page 22.     transit and pedestrian supportive development and a range of housing options through intensification, redevelopment and infill development; and     additional residential growth and development through various means including, but not limited to, financial incentives and reduced development standards. The City will also encourage the expansion of SDAs by:     Improving   connectivity   and   active   transportation   networks   within   the Strategic Development Areas and adjacent neighbourhoods; and     promoting the establishment of Neighbourhood Commercial in areas that contain medium to high density residential but few local convenience and neighbourhood commercial uses within a safe-walkable distance. Strategic Development Areas  Strategic Development Areas (SDAs) are areas within the Urban Settlement Area that will  accommodate   a   significant   portion   of   the   City’s   growth   through   intensification. Intensification is essential to  completing   our   n ei ghb ourhoods , making the most   efficient   use of   land,   resources,  infrastructure and public service facilities, minimizing negative impacts on air quality and  climate   change,   promoting   energy   efficiency   and   supporting   public   transit,   active  transportation and the effici ent movement of goods.  The City’s SDAs comprise the first settlement area of the City (including Downtown) and  areas within a safe - walkable distance to an array of services and amenities such as retail  clusters, grocery stores, community centres, schools, and parks. Residential develop ment in the First  Neighbourhoods also stimulates increased investment ,   business activity , and   downtown  revitalization.  Strategic Development Areas   -   Other  The other identified SDAs are those that have significant development potential to become  mixed - use neighbourhoods with pedestrian - friendly access to a variety of services,  amenities, and housing within a safe walkable distance. BACKGROUND  In 2016, City Council approved application A-14-16-Z.OP to permit commercial uses , more specifically a “Social Innovation Hub”   and residential uses in the existing building; and to reduce required parking from 37 to 21 spaces. ANALYSIS Conformity with Official Plan  The applicant is proposing to convert the basement of the existing building at 267 Cathcart Street into a shared office space, intended for individuals who may not have a corporate or business office, but wish to have access to office equipment and a collaborative work environment. The land use map of the Official Plan (Schedule C) designates the subject property (267 Cathcart Street) as Residential. Residential lands are intended primarily for  residential uses and to facilitate the creation of “complete neighbourhoods,” by  providing a variety of housing types and densities, as well as neighbourhood- oriented commercial uses. The proposed development seeks additional office space   making   the   development   more   commercial   in   nature   therefore,   it   is  Page 445 of 983 A-7-24-Z.OP   –   267 Cathcart Street & 159 John Street May 13, 2024 Page 3 .  appropriate to re-designate 267 Cathcart Street to reflect the planned use of the property. Commercial land uses include industries engaged in retail, business, finance, insurance and real estate, among others. The commercial land use designation is consistent with the nature of the proposed development. The subject property and existing building are well placed to operate as a commercial hub within the neighbourhood, and the proposed office uses, which are currently creative in nature, do not negatively impact the surrounding neighbourhood and have the potential to act as a catalyst towards re-investment into the neighbourhood.   The applicant has indicated her vision for the area is that of a creative hub, including mixed use live/work spaces with a vibrant creative mentality. The renovations also include a full kitchen, which the applicant has indicated could be utilized as a community kitchen.   It is therefore appropriate to re-designate the property to commercial. Policy C.4 of the Official Plan requires major office space to be located in the downtown area. The Zoning By-law defines major office space as greater than 300 m 2 . This policy was originally intended to maintain the downtown area as the primary   administrative   centre   of   the   community.   The   application   proposes approximately 640 m 2   of additional office space outside the downtown area and therefore requires a textual amendment to the Official Plan to permit the proposed office size. The additional office space would occupy the basement of the existing building. The current definition of major office space (300m 2 ) is too small. Office Uses (and other relatively small office spaces, such as medical offices), should be spread throughout the community. Furthermore, the 2016 Downtown Strategy places greater emphasis on making downtown more of a complete neighbourhood, with additional residential, cultural and recreational development, while at the same time preserving the downtown as the administrative core of the community. Approval of this application is appropriate and consistent with the current vision for the Downtown. The 2022 draft Official Plan proposes to increase the maximum size of office space outside the downtown from 300m 2   to 700m 2 . This would allow a broader range of office types and sizes to be located outside of the downtown, to address vacancies in other commercial areas, support the adaptive reuse of vacant commercial buildings and promote greater access to services. The proposed increase to the minimum size of major office space is consistent with how the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation (MPAC) defines major office space. Both subject properties are within 150m of the defined Downtown area.   The overall built form of the area is dense, characterized by relatively small lots, high lot coverage and minimal setbacks, consistent with the built form found in the defined downtown area, which is not surprising given that both areas developed at roughly the same time. The subject properties are located in the First Neighbourhoods Strategic Growth Area which will include the most regulatory flexibility and highest incentive levels. In addition, the First Neighbourhood Area would essentially result in combining this neighbourhood, and others, with the currently defined downtown area. COMMENTS  This application proposes to construct a   “Co -working Space ” also known as a  shared office space between different individuals who may not work for the same employer.   The proposed renovations will occur within the basement level of the existing building at 267 Cathcart Street. The main floor of the building is currently occupied by the offices of a marketing firm and an architectural office. The Commercial Transitional Zone (CT2) was initially designed as a hybrid commercial/residential zone to occupy the northern portions of the Downtown area, north of Queen Street to Wellington Street, where there is a combination of residential dwellings and lighter commercial uses, such as office uses, which in many cases occupy converted dwellings.   Since the inception of the CT2 Zone, it has also been utilized as a neighbourhood commercial zone to permit a variety of  Page 447 of 983 A-7-24-Z.OP   –   267 Cathcart Street & 159 John Street May 13, 2024 Page 5 .  lighter commercial uses in residential areas. As such, the scope of permitted uses in the CT2 Zone are compatible with surrounding residential uses. With this said, parking is a potential concern.   Currently, 267 Cathcart Street requires and supplies 22 parking spaces. Upon further review of this application the   proposed   development   requires   an   additional   13   parking   spaces.   The applicant proposes to locate 7 of these spaces at 159 John Street, which is approximately 50m east of the proposed new office space.   Furthermore, the applicant proposes to reduce the remaining required parking by 6 spaces. The applicant has indicated that in her experience, the parking lot at 267 Cathcart Street is never near full capacity. As part of the review of this application, planning staff visited the site on 8 separate occasions, on different days and at different times of the day, and between 5-9 vehicles were parked on the lot at any one time. Planning staff is currently working on parking reforms, aimed at reducing parking requirements across the City, with the greatest reductions proposed for the downtown and first neighbourhood areas.   It is likely that upon approval of recommended reforms, the current on-site parking at 267 Cathcart Street will conform. Furthermore, on-street parking is available on both sides of Cathcart Street, and based upon various site visits conducted by staff, such on-street parking is not being utilized at very high rates. Given the commercial nature of the proposed uses, overnight parking during winter months will not be an issue, should the street be required to accommodate overflow parking.   Furthermore, on-street parking is well within the denser urban nature of this neighbourhood. With all of this in mind, and based upon further review, staff is no longer of the opinion that 159 John Street is required to accommodate satellite parking.   The Building Division has indicated that placing a parking lot at 159 John Street, which was intended to be temporary to determine parking demand, would trigger the need for a record of site condition should future residential development be proposed. The applicant has future development plans for this property that would be impacted by the need to undertake a record of site condition.   The property is a corner lot with high visibility and as such, should be developed at a higher use that will have greater benefits to the surrounding community. The applicant is agreeable to this approach. Staff also recommend amending the existing special exception zoning by repealing clauses 1 and 2, which permit 16 dwelling units within the existing building and scope commercial usage to the offices of a marketing firm and architecture firm only.   The proposed CT2 zoning already permits a wide variety of dwelling units subject to performance standards and a defined building envelope. Furthermore, given   the   proposed   change   to   a   more   commercial   zoning,   it   is   no   longer  Page 448 of 983 A-7-24-Z.OP   –   267 Cathcart Street & 159 John Street May 13, 2024 Page 6 .  appropriate to scope office uses to specific businesses.   As previously noted, the CT2 Zone contains uses that are compatible with nearby residences. It is also noted that in a Vacant Land Condo lots are referred to as units. As part of the plan registration process, the City is required to sign a declaration stating there are sufficient funds available to complete all common elements prior to registration. In this case, the City becomes the surety to guarantee that lots will be serviced and all common elements will be constructed. Therefore, 100% financial   guarantee   will   be   required   prior   to   registering   any   parts   of   the condominium plan. A stormwater management pond is proposed as a common element at the southeast corner of the site. A 1.5m sidewalk will be provided on the south side of the private access road to provide pedestrian access to the site. All individual dwelling units in the Draft Plan will be provided with personal amenity space, therefore cash in lieu of parkland is recommended. Sussex Park is located northeast of the subject property, and is within a safe walkable distance of the proposed development. Conditions of Draft Plan approval also require the collection of a per lot fee for the purposes of the City planting a tree on each lot of the subdivision. Where an owner does not wish to have a tree planted, the funds go into a reserve for tree planting in other parts of the City. The design   was   based on an   iterative   process   in   which different outlet conditions,   pond  depth   /   storage relationships were   analyzed.  lnflow   hydrographs   were   generated   in   the   Visual   OTTHYMO   model. Storage   discharge relationships were   generated   for   the   pond with   the   use   of a spreadsheet.   The storage   discharge  relationships were   then   input into corresponding separate   reservoir   routing functions   in Visual  OTTHYMO.   The   appropriate   inflow hydrographs   were then   connected   to the reservoirs   in   Visual  OTTHYMO. Visual OTTHYMO then performed reservoir routing routines producing   attenuated  outflow   hydrographs. Equitable Housing and Legal Considerations  Rooming Houses are defined in the Zoning By- law as “ Establishments primarily engaged in providing temporary or longer-term accommodation, which for the period of occupancy, may serve as a principal residence. ” Rooming houses are  homes in which private rooms are rented as opposed to an entire house/apartment dwelling. They typically consist of private rooms with shared facilities such as kitchens, bathrooms and common areas. There is a distinction between a rooming house and merely a group of friends/co- workers, etc. renting a home. Below are some examples of established criteria that has been used to distinguish a group-rented home from a rooming house:     All of the tenants in the dwelling unit know each other in advance of signing their lease;     No keyed locks on any bedroom doors;     The tenants enter into a group lease and pay the rent as a group;     The tenants are responsible for cleaning the entire home; and     There have been no renovations to increase the number of bedrooms in the home. Rooming houses are one of the most affordable living accommodations available, thus they not only play a critical role in the housing market but also represent the only housing option available to low-income individuals who are faced with precarious shelter situations or homelessness. They have also increasingly been used to meet short-term accommodation needs, such as the case with students and working professionals who may intend to locate in the city temporarily.  Page 528 of 983 A-6-24-Z 26 Queen Street East May 13, 2024 Page 6 .  In discussions with the applicant, it was noted that there is a high demand for the rooming house, with a wait-list already in place for prospective tenants. Interest spans   across   various   demographics,   including   students   and   health-care professionals. By-laws and policies that regulate rooming houses require careful consideration to ensure that they are based on legitimate land use planning grounds and that they  do not amount to “people zoning”.   This term refers to the prohibition of certain uses based   solely   on   the   expected   tenant   demographics,   rather   than   evaluating proposals against established planning criteria such as building specifications, density, infrastructure provision, traffic impact, etc. As rooming houses often cater to individuals with lower incomes, attempts to restrict their development without a valid land use planning rationale could amount to   “ people zoning ” , which could disproportionally impact vulnerable individuals from accessing housing. This could be in contravention of the Human Rights Code. There are a number of examples across Ontario where municipalities have passed by-laws   to   restrict   alternative   housing   developments   by   outright   prohibition, minimum distance separations, caps, and quotas, only to have them turned down by both the Ontario Land Tribunal and the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario. Such by-laws   were   found   to   have   prevented   equal   housing   opportunity   and disproportionally impacted Class-protected individuals. The proposed development, a higher-density residential property, is located on the western edge of the downtown area, is adjacent to a major road (Queen Street), is within walking distance to the Dennis Street public transit station, various social services, and commercial establishments, including Station Mall. Nearby uses include a film production company, an auto repair shop, pet grooming services,   second-hand   goods   store,   cannabis   dispensary,   uniform   cleaning services, coffee shop, and a number of under-utilized parking spaces. This area is also zoned to permit high density residential development in addition to other non- residential uses. The proposed development is compatible with the area.  Commercial Function and Vibrancy of Queen Street  A large portion of the downtown area, including the properties that front Queen Street, are C2 zoned. The C2 zone only permits residential uses on upper stories, with the intent that the ground floor will be maintained for commercial purposes. Planning staff acknowledge that converting ground floor commercial spaces to non-commercial uses can have an impact on the commercial function and vibrancy of the downtown area. Some of these impacts include the loss of economic activity  Page 529 of 983 A-6-24-Z 26 Queen Street East May 13, 2024 Page 7 .  in the downtown, impact on local businesses, and change in downtown character; however, no negative impacts are anticipated from the approval of this application for the following reasons:     The applicant has noted that attracting a commercial business has been difficult, resulting in the continued vacancy of the premises. A conversion would not detract from existing commercial demand.     There is no prevailing trend of ground-floor commercial conversions to residential units.   Every conversion   request must proceed through   the rezoning process and obtain Council approval. If there does become a concern, Planning staff will seek to implement an interim control by-law to freeze such development proposals to allow staff an opportunity to assess the situation. This type of development activity will be monitored by Planning staff.     With the exception of the nearby restaurant establishments that contribute to   the   night-time   economy   and   vibrancy   of   this   area,   much   of   the surrounding land uses include parking lots and offices that do not operate into the evening. A residential conversion will not negatively impact the character or vibrancy of the area. In fact, it may further activate the downtown during the evening or create demand for further commercial uses.     The residential conversion will reduce vacant space, addressing associated concerns of building blight and neglect, safety issues as a result of empty buildings, reduced foot traffic and vibrancy. These positive contributions outweigh potential concerns. While the draft Official Plan acknowledges the importance of office space, it recognizes   that   activating   the   Downtown   beyond   typical   business   hours   is essential for a vibrant downtown. The proposed development strikes a balance between these needs, contributing to the area's improvement.  Residential Interface  A key consideration when permitting residential uses on the ground floor of commercial corridors is that the building design ensures that tenants are afforded a high degree of privacy from the street, and that the building interface does not aesthetically impact the character of the commercial corridor. The ground floor of the building, originally designed for commercial use, will retain its large storefront windows. No dwelling units will directly abut Queen Street; instead, a vestibule or lobby will separate the units from the street, addressing privacy concerns. A site-specific special exception will enforce this arrangement.  Page 530 of 983 A-6-24-Z 26 Queen Street East May 13, 2024 Page 8 .  The illuminated entranceway and lobby described by the applicant can enhance "social surveillance," making the Queen Street public space feel safer and more active, therefore benefiting the commercial streetscape. SUMMARY  The applicant, PHG Renos (c/o Mehdi Arfaei), has submitted an application for a site-specific amendment to the Zoning By-law, seeking the approval to permit a rooming house to occupy both the upper storey and ground floor of the existing building. Rooming homes are an essential housing alternative and play a pivotal role in providing   affordable   accommodation.   Evaluating   these   housing   development proposals must be based on established land use planning principles without discriminating against potential tenant demographics. The   proposed   property   is   a   suitable   location   for   higher-density   residential development due to the character of the area and its access to nearby amenities and services. Concerns   about   converting   commercial   space   to   non-commercial   uses   in downtown areas relate to potential impacts on economic activity, local businesses, and community character; however, planning staff do not anticipate these impacts with the approval of this application. Instead, the proposal will enhance this part of the downtown by re-purposing a vacant building.  Page 531 of 983 A-6-24-Z 26 Queen Street East May 13, 2024 Page 9 .  The applicant plans to preserve the storefront windows and create a lobby entrance, contributing to a sense of "social surveillance" along Queen Street and improving   the area’s vibrancy and safety.  Planning staff support this proposal. Marie   Rooftop Solar Photovoltaic System at Transit  Services, Public Works and Transportation, and  West End Community Centre  AECOM SSM Solar Rooftop Report Feb   2011   Rev . 1.Docx  AECOM was retained by the City of Sault Ste. Marie (City) to carry out a review of the structural implications and feasibility of installing solar generating panels on the roofs of several City buildings. The buildings that have been included in the study include the Transit bus repair and storage building on Huron Street, the Works garage facility on Sackville Road, and the proposed new West End Community Centre (WECC). The solar generating systems would be c onstructed within the terms of the Government of Ontario‟s Feed In Tariff program that establishes long  term contracts for electrical generation from renewable sources. The study included a structural review of the existing roof components at the Transit and Works buildings to determine if the roof could support new solar generating systems. This work involved a visual inspection of the roofing structural components, detailed measurements of the structural components, and a structural evaluation of the capacity of the system to support additional loading. At the WECC the building has been designed to support a solar generating system on the south facing portion of the sloped roof over the soccer fields and so a further structural review of this building was not included in our scope. On the basis of the potential for additional weight   that could be supported by the buildings‟ roof structure   a possible solar generating system was selected and a size of a system was determined for each building. The capital cost of each generating system was estimated and the implications of connecting the solar generating system to existing electrical systems at each building were considered. The electrical generating potential and anticipated revenue for each system was determined and the relative pay back for installing a solar generating system at each building was evaluated. At the Transit building it is estimated that a 160 kW solar panel system could be installed for an estimated cost of $1,650,000 not including the roof replacement costs but including allowances for contingencies and engineering. The anticipated annual generation should be 187,000 kWhrs for anticipated annual revenue of about $133,000. The straight line pay back period is 12.4 years not including the influence of interest costs. Prior to installing a solar system on the roof areas it is recommended that the roofing membrane at the Transit building repair and storage bays should be replaced. The estimated cost to replace the roofing is $780,000 including contingencies and engineering. The total cost for the roof replacement and solar generating system is estimated to be $2,430,000. At the Works garage building it is estimated that a 60 kW solar panel system can be installed. It is determined that the main roof area is not structurally adequate to support a large scale array of solar panels on the roof, and a solar generating system including rows of panels along the south wall face and two rows of panels on the roof at the south edge of the roof are structurally feasible. It is estimated that the overall cost for a solar system, excluding upgrading the existing south wall is $626,000. The anticipated annual generation should be 66,000 kWhrs for anticipated annual revenue of about $47,000. The straight line pay back period is 13.3 years, not including the influence of interest costs. The estimated cost to upgrade the wall system is $216,000 including contingencies and engineering. The total cost for the wall upgrade and solar generating system is estimated to be $842,000. At the WECC it is concluded that a 240 kW solar panel system can be installed at the south facing roof over the soccer fields. It is estimated that the solar generating system will cost $1,462,000 including contingencies and engineering. The anticipated annual generation should be 197,400 kWhrs for anticipated annual revenue of about $140,700. The straight line pay back period is 10.4 years not including the influence of interest costs. In addition to the conclusions related to the solar generating systems several recommendations are presented in the report with respect to maintenance or upgrading of roofing and wall systems at the Transit and Works buildings. In particular the roofing at the Transit building should be replaced in the near future, and the south wall cladding system at the Works building should be replaced and upgraded. Where the evaluation concluded that the existing roofing components are not considered structurally adequate for the proposed solar systems and current Code requirements, options to upgrade or modify the existing or proposed new components have been developed and evaluated. f. In 2009, the Government of Ontario announced a Feed In Tariff (FIT) program that allows building owners to install solar generating panels and sell the electricity into the grid. The rates to be paid for the generated electricity vary. For typical roof mounted systems that are larger than 10kW, the feed in rate currently varies from 71.3 cents per kilowatt hour (c/kwh) to 53.9 c/kwh depending on the size of the facility. A copy of the FIT price structure is attached in Appendix A. Solar photovoltaic panels are typically about 1.7 m by 1 m in area. The panels generally can generate between 200 and 250 Watts, per panel depending on the manufacturer and style of panel, and recently higher generation capacity panels are being manufactured. Panels typically weigh around 24 kg., and have a unit weight of approximately 0.14 kN/m 2   (3 pounds per square foot). The weight of the panels and supporting frames on the roof structure will vary depending on the slope and spacing of panels and type of support frame required. For example, panels installed on a sloping roof require only two rails along the roof below the panels for attachment, whereas panels installed on a flat roof require a support framework to secure the panels at the correct angle. For the purposes of this study, we have based sizes of systems and electrical generation on 250 W panels. Other sizes of panels, and system capacities may be selected during detailed design, however the 250 W panel size should provide a comparable installation cost at this time.  The orientation of roof mounted solar panels can result in additional loading on the roof structure. At a minimum, the self weight, or dead load, of the panels and support frames will be imposed on the structure. In addition, increased snow accumulation may occur and will depend on the orientation of the panels, their height above the roof, and slope of the panels relative to the roof. The panel installation that will cause the least loading on the roof system is installation on an existing sloping roof. In this case, the panel system weight will include the weight of the panels plus the support rails. This type of system is considered to impose an additional dead load of about 0.19 kN/m 2   (4 psf). When the panels are installed on an  Page 886 of 983 AECOM   The City of Sault Ste. Marie   Rooftop Solar Photovoltaic System at Transit  Services, Public Works and Transportation, and  West End   Community Centre  4  existing sloping roof, the panels are placed with a gap of about 50 to 100 mm between the panels and roof surface. With this installation, no new or additional snow loading is caused by the panels. It is noted that on many existing sloped roofs the solar panels are supported on rails that extend horizontally along the roof. The rail system has a self weight that is in addition to the self weight of the panels. At the WECC the panels can be installed using a special clip that connects to the standing seam of the metal roof and a system of rails is not considered to be necessary. In this case the specified loading of 3 psf is sufficient for the panel system. When the panel installation is on an existing flat roof area, the panels need to be installed at a slope to have exposure to the sun and therefore become an obstruction on the roof that can potentially increase snow accumulation. The added loading of the snow accumulation must be supported by the roof structure in addition to the increased dead loading of the panels and their support frames. If the roof structure has sufficient residual capacity that exceeds the basic snow loading and original roof system dead load, support for additional solar panel dead loads and snow accumulation is possible. However, the additional snow accumulation loading may be significant and most roof structures will not be designed with the required reserves in structural capacity. As part of this study, options have been considered that minimize additional snow accumulation resulting from the solar panels.  1.4.1   Installation Option A: Low Profile  One method to install solar panels and avoid additional snow accumulation is to install the panels at a height lower than the depth of the basic snow accumulation   so that they do not form an „obstruction‟.   In the case of snow loads in Sault Ste. Marie, any panels installed with a height not exceeding about 830 mm above the roof will not cause additional snow accumulation. In this case, the roof structure will need to support the dead load of the panels and support frames only. Reinforcing the existing structure may therefore be minimal, or not required. There are, however, several disadvantages to a low profile installation. During winter, it is likely that the panels will become snow covered. For a large installation, removing the snow is impractical. The potential electrical generation during winter months would then be lost when the panels are snow covered. It is noted that electrical generation during winter is modest relative to the months of March through September when there are more sunlight hours. The lost generation capacity would need to be compared with the increased costs to install the panels at greater heights that will lead to snow accumulation and thereby require reinforcing the existing roof structure. Another disadvantage to a low profile installation is that the panel angle will be low, around 15 0 . At this angle, the panels will generate power at approximately 5.6% less than panels installed at a more favourable 40 0   angle. With a low profile installation, replacing the roof membrane will also require that the panels be removed to gain access to the membrane. Also, maintenance of the membrane may be more difficult since areas under the panels will not be easily accessible.  1.4.2   Installation Option B- Raised Frames  Another method of installing solar panels is to provide a support framework that elevates the panels sufficiently high above the roof so that increased accumulation does not occur. In this case, the snow below the panels is considered to be scoured away by wind, and no increase in snow load needs to be considered. While this scenario is recognized in general terms in the current Code, specific prescriptive design parameters are not provided. However, some recommendations and guidance is provided in documents referenced in the Code. For the purpose of this study, it has been considered that panels installed above a level of 2 m above the roof will not result in increased snow accumulation. This concept may need to be developed further as the Code requirements are not clear at this time and new information is being considered by authorities. The panels would likely be visible from the ground level and some people may consider the panel installation unsightly. For the purposes of our study at this time, we will consider the cost implications of the raised frame installation when comparing various options. The design of the frames also must take into account wind forces and the resultant loading on the supporting building structure.  The solar generating panels on a flat roof need to be supported above the roof and should be oriented at an angle to be exposed to sunlight. It has generally been considered that two methods are possible to support the panels, one is a ballasted system and one will involve a system of supports that are anchored into the existing roof support structure. The anchored supports require that the solar panel structural supports extend down through the roof membrane to connect to the roof structure. The supports need to be provided with flashings to the roofing membrane. A ballasted system does not require penetrations through the roof and usually consists of concrete blocks added to the panel support system to hold the panels down in high winds. Each system has benefits and drawbacks that are discussed in the following sections.  1.5.1   Ballasted Support Frames  Solar panels supported on a flat roof will be exposed to wind loading. Depending on the slope of the panels and the height above the roof structure, the wind loading will tend to lift the panels. For roof areas in Sault Ste. Marie, the uplift load on roof mounted panels will require a ballast weight of a minimum of about 0.65 kN/m 2   (13.6 psf) for the panel area. The wind uplift force increases as the slope of the panels increases and so the weight indicated is considered as a minimum. The typical type of ballast consists of concrete blocks or slabs that are placed on the support frame for the panels. The support frame rests directly on the roofing membrane, with padding to protect the membrane from damage by the frames.  1.5.2   Connected Support Frames  With a connected structural support frame for the panels, a system of supports is connected through the roofing membrane and secured to the existing roof structural system. There are numerous different configurations that could be used to support the frames and panels. The structural supports would depend on the type of underlying structural framing and the type of panel installation (either raised frames or low profile installation). For installing a low profile panel system or a series of raised frames, it would most likely require installation of a continuous curb along the roof to distribute the weight of the panels, and permit anchorage to the existing structure. Depending on the structural capacity of the existing framing system, a connected support frame can be installed in two general configurations. If the roof has the capacity to support the weight of the solar panels and frames, then the panels can be supported on curbs connected to the existing structure. The panels may need to be supported on frames at a height that does not attract or cause additional snow accumulation. Installing the curbs and connecting to the existing roof structure involves significant changes to the roofing membrane since the curbs need to be placed at relatively close spacing. Typically, the existing vertical support structure (columns and foundations) have additional reserve capacity. If it is determined that the existing horizontal structural components (joists, trusses and beams) do not have capacity to support the additional weight of the panel system, a new elevated support structure can be introduced. Marie urge the Province of Ontario to recognize the physician shortage in Sault Ste. Marie and Ontario, to fund health care appropriately, and ensure every Ontarian has access to physician care. Hollingsworth Whereas the waterfront and local marinas are an important part of our  Page 10 of 533 community; and Whereas garbage, plastic waste, discarded cigarette butts, and other debris find their way into our water systems by various means including littering, blowing winds, and accidental means; and Whereas it is said that 8 million tonnes of plastic waste end up in our oceans every year and it is incumbent on us to protect our local water systems to keep them clear of garbage, plastic waste, cigarette butts, and other debris; and Whereas the waterfront and marinas in Sault Ste. Marie are often prone to collecting garbage, plastic waste, cigarette butts, and other debris that floats in the water systems causing potential damage to the ecosystem; and Whereas “Seabins” are floating trash skimmers that take in debris and trash- filled water through a pump to retain the trash in a catch bag while returning clean water to the waterway; and Whereas “Seabins” are a known product that, when used strategically can help to keep garbage out of the environment by intercepting trash that has made its way into the water ecosystem; and Whereas Oceans Plastic Clean Up . Com advises that “Seabins” can help capture   approximately   3.9   kgs   of   trash   per   day   or   1.4   tons   per   year, eliminating the waste from our waterways to help protect our environment Now Therefore Be It Resolved that staff be requested to review the process of installing “Seabins” at local marinas and strategic waterfront areas and report back with a plan to implement the installation before the end of the 2024 season. 9.2   Bike Valets Mover Councillor A. Caputo Seconder Councillor S. Spina Whereas bike valets provide a secure, supervised areas to leave bicycles; and Whereas The Soo Moves Plan aims to help make it easier to walk or bike in the City, providing residents and visitors with new ways to connect with the community at a human scale; and Whereas   many   people   cite   bike   theft   as   a   reason   they   do   not   bike   to destinations in the downtown; and Whereas   according   to   Square   One   Insurance   Services,   bicycle   thefts increased by 429 per cent in Victoria, Vancouver, Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg, Toronto, and Montreal; and Whereas quality of life is listed as a pillar in the City’s strategic plan and increasing the opportunity to safely bike within our city increases quality of life advantages while also contributing to having vibrant downtown areas  Page 11 of 533 Now Therefore Be It Resolved that staff be requested to research and report back on a pilot project of bike valets in key downtown areas in Sault Ste. Marie during the summer months. 9.3   Ronald A. Irwin Civic Centre Seventh Floor Space Mover Councillor L. Vezeau-Allen Seconder Councillor S. Hollingsworth Whereas the Ronald A. Irwin Civic Centre is located on our waterfront, and whereas the property hosts beautiful views of our river and surrounding naturescape; and Whereas the property has panoramic views from its seventh floor; and Whereas vacant space exists on the property; and Whereas the City currently holds third party leases with several businesses on its properties; including the Ice Breaker Bar and Grill at the John Rhodes Community Centre; and Whereas much consultation and consideration is currently underway to improve and develop economically our most treasured asset; and Whereas multiple celebrations and events have been held in the existing spaces at the Ronald A. Irwin Civic Centre; and Whereas the potential to have a multi-use event space available to public enterprise has not been examined; Now Therefore Be It Resolved that staff be requested to undertake an inspection of the seventh floor space and bring a report to Council regarding a possible business plan to create a commercial space within the Ronald A. Irwin Civic Centre. 9.4   Self-Cleaning Public Toilets Mover Councillor L. Vezeau-Allen Seconder Councillor A. Caputo Whereas in our community and many others the populations of those who are homeless   or   precariously   housed   have   been   on   the   increase,   adding pressures on agencies that serve the most vulnerable; and Whereas the reality of having access to clean and safe toileting facilities has been identified as need across our service agencies; and Whereas while our City has publicly accessible washrooms at various locations, including: Dennis Street Bus Terminal, GFL Memorial Gardens, Downtown Plaza, Roberta Bondar Pavilion and through our District Social Services at the Community Resource Centre, these facilities are not open or available on a 24-hour, 7-day a week basis; and Whereas the general public and tourists alike also need access to washroom  Page 12 of 533 facilities outside regular business hours of public facilities; and Whereas since 1992 vandal-proof, self-cleaning toilets have been available in Europe; and Whereas in cities such as Montreal, Valemount B.C. and soon, Waterloo Ontario, have public accessible free self-cleaning toilets Now Therefore Be It Resolved that staff be requested to research and connect with social services agencies to seek input and plan for possible self-cleaning toilet facilities in our community and provide Council with a report, including potential locations, cost and maintenance responsibilities. 10. Spina  Whereas the state of health care in Ontario is in crisis, with 2.3 million Ontarians lacking access to a family doctor, emergency room closures across the province, patients being de-rostered and 40% of family doctors considering retirement over the next five years; and  Page 47 of 533 May 13, 2024 Council Minutes  23  Whereas the Northern Ontario School of Medicine University says communities in northern Ontario are short more than 350 physicians, including more than 200 family doctors; and half of the physicians working in northern Ontario are expected to retire in the next five years; and  Whereas the Ontario Medical Association and the Province of Ontario were negotiating a funding agreement to improve access, reduce wait times, and to help encourage physicians to enter the areas of practice most in need; and  Whereas the percentage of family physicians practicing comprehensive family medicine has declined from 77% in 2008 to 65% in 2022; and  Whereas per capita health-care spending in Ontario is the lowest of all provinces in Canada, and  Whereas the Government of Ontario recently submitted arguments to an arbitrator stating "there is no concern of a diminished supply of physicians", ignoring the real needs of communities across the province including Sault Ste. Marie and every Ontarian without access to a physician;  Now Therefore Be It Resolved that the Council of the City of Sault Ste. Marie urge the Province of Ontario to recognize the physician shortage in Sault Ste. Marie and Ontario, to fund health care appropriately, and ensure every Ontarian has access to physician care. Schell, CPA, CA, Chief Financial Officer & Treasurer  DEPARTMENT:   Corporate Services  RE:   Cancellation of Vacant Unit Rebate  ________________________________________________________________  Purpose  The purpose of this report is to seek Council approval to eliminate the Vacant Unit Rebate provided to the Commercial property class.  Background  On June 12, 2017 Council approved changes to the Vacant Unit Rebate as a result of a provincial legislative change that provided municipalities flexibility to tailor the program to their local circumstances. Prior to the changes the budget for the annual rebates was approximately $375,000, with 120 properties receiving the rebate. The changes to the program included:     Ending the rebate eligibility for the Industrial property class. An Economic Growth Community Improvement Plan replaced the vacancy rebate and encourages new industrial development     Ending the rebate eligibility for Shopping Centres, which will have vacancies from time to time as part of their business model     Restricting   the   Commercial   class   rebates   (the   only   qualifying   class remaining for the rebate) to a maximum of 3 taxation years for each 10 year period.     Temporary uses were introduced that allowed uses of any type that do not pay rent not be considered as a break in the three consecutive month requirement.   This   was   hoped   to   encourage   new   start-up   business, temporary uses and window displays.  Analysis  The annual vacancy rebate has steadily decreased since the changes were instituted in 2017. Prior to implementing the changes in 2017 the average annual rebate for the municipal share of taxes was $375,000, as compared to $23,900 in 2022 (rebated in 2023). This is a 94% decrease in 6 years. With the restriction of a maximum of 3 taxation years for each 10 year period many of the historically  Page 103 of 533 Cancellation of Vacancy Rebate June 24, 2024 Page 2.  consistent applications have been eliminated. In 2024, seven (7) applications were processed, of which only three (3) were first time applications.  Staff are recommending that the Vacancy Rebate Program be eliminated effective July 1, 2024 based upon the following:     There are relatively few property owners for a proportionately larger cost to administer the program     The rebate has phased itself out over the last 6 years with very few new applications     The rebate did not encourage occupancy or temporary use as anticipated     The rebates are effectively funded by the rest of the property tax base.     A vacant home tax has been approved for the residential class. A rebate for the commercial class, which also has problematic vacancies, is inconsistent with the direction for residential properties.     Certain vacant commercial properties could be converted to accommodate much needed residential units.     Planning reports, such as the housing needs assessment, have shown that Sault Ste. Marie has entered a period of growth, and it is anticipated that the community will continue to grow, including commercial growth and a reduction in commercial vacancies.  The Province of Ontario in their 2018 budget stated that greater flexibility was provided   to   municipalities   to   tailor   their   programs   to   best   reflect   local circumstances and interests of local businesses. While municipalities that decided to modify their vacancy programs at that time had implemented a variety of changes, 80% of those municipalities phased out the program by 2020. The recommendation proposed by staff is consistent with the direction taken by many other municipalities.  Financial Implications  The 2024 annual operating budget for vacancy rebates is $100,000. If the rebate is eliminated effective July 1, 2024, there will be a savings of $100,000 to the 2025 tax levy. Background  Under section 357 of the   Municipal Act, 2001,   taxpayers may make an application for the cancellation, reduction or refund of taxes in response to changes in assessment facts concerning the property. The reduction reduces the taxes to the correct and proper amount. Applications have been made by staff or the property owner and have been reviewed by Municipal Property Assessment Corporation (MPAC) to verify the assessment values and taxation periods to be used for the adjustment.  Section 358 of the   Municipal Act   permits applications for tax adjustments related to taxes levied in each or either of the two years preceding the year in which the application is made who are overcharged by reason of any gross or manifest error in the preparation of the assessment roll by the Municipal Property Assessment Corporation that was an error of fact. This may include, but not limited to, clerical errors, the transposition of figure or typographical errors, but not an error in judgement in making the assessment upon which the taxes have been levied. These applications relate to taxes levied in each of the of the two preceding years in which the application was made.  Section 354(2)(b) of the   Municipal Act , authorizes the removal of unpaid taxes from the tax roll if the taxes are no longer payable as a result of tax relief under section 358. One of the properties listed for adjustment under section 358 was due to an error that occurred in 2016. The application under 358 reduces the taxes levied for the current and two preceding years; 2022-2024. Section 354(2)(b) reduces the previous years taxes levied from 2016-2021.  The listing of adjustments of realty taxes pursuant to section 354, 357 and 358 of the   Municipal Act   is attached to this report.
